Need to search first.I've written notes on all 20 verses from the pages I could read. Some areas are thin, though. My search tool hit its usage limit partway through, and after that I couldn't open more pages. Most of what follows comes from Enduring Word, Matthew Henry, Precept Austin, The Gospel Coalition, a Desiring God sermon, and the multi-commentary pages on BibleHub and StudyLight. Those pages bring together Gill, Barnes, Calvin, Clarke, Benson, Poole, Keil & Delitzsch, Coffman, Constable, Smith and others.

**Not found:** I reached no Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist (seedbed/wesley.nnu), NET Bible note, Bible Odyssey, Spurgeon or Pentecostal-denomination pages. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of Micah 7. Where I give a tradition label, it's the one StudyLight itself prints next to the commentator.

---

## Part 1: The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Micah speaks for the sinful nation and confesses that its sin has left it poor, with no fruit left to enjoy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Clarke says the prophet feels like a lone grape that escaped the harvest. He longed for outstanding godliness ("first-ripe fruit") but found only a weak or fake kind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-1.html
- Barnes links this to Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isa 5:7). Isaiah said Israel gave wild grapes; Micah says only a few poor gleanings are left. (same URL)
- Calvin admits some read the verse as grief over punishment. He thinks v. 2 shows it is about the people's wickedness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/micah/7.htm
- Trapp hears the prophet grieving that his preaching has had so little success, and he compares Isaiah 24:13, 16. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/mic-7.cfm
- A note on BibleHub explains the picture: good people, who once came "in clusters," are now single berries scattered here and there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Matthew Henry says people treat each other like prey, lying in wait like lions. They will ruin anyone's life or livelihood to get rich. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- Precept Austin notes that the Greek Old Testament uses a word for complete denial ("no one at all"), and a word for setting an ambush. It also compares sin crouching at the door in Genesis 4. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_7_commentary
- A BibleHub note says the Hebrew word for "godly man" means someone pious, kind and generous. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-1.htm

**v. 3**
- Henry gives two readings. In one, they do evil skilfully with both hands. In the other, they are quick to do harm, while the prince and judge do good only when paid. He takes "they weave it together" to mean they tangle a case until justice gets lost. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- The BibleHub chapter study says leaders and judges are corrupt, take bribes and plot together. https://biblehub.com/micah/7.htm

**v. 4**
- Constable says even the best people were like briers that snag and hurt anyone who comes close. God's watchmen, the prophets, had warned of punishment, but no one listened. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-4.html
- Barnes says that when even the good are corrupt, sin is "full." The judgment the prophets foresaw comes suddenly, and he compares 1 Thessalonians 5:3. (same URL, and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-4.htm)
- Clarke says nothing will stay "wrapped up" on that day; everything will be laid open. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-4.html
- The Pulpit Commentary, as given on BibleHub, notes a wordplay in the Hebrew: they were a thorn hedge (*mesukah*), and they will fall into confusion (*mebukah*). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-4.htm
- Guzik says sinners feel they will never pay, but a day of reckoning still comes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/

**v. 5**
- Guzik says selfishness had destroyed trust, so no one could rely on a friend or even family. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Henry says decent people keep a friend's secrets, and these people no longer did. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- A note on BibleHub quotes Dionysius: we shouldn't become suspicious of everyone because of such verses, only careful. It compares 1 John 4:1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-6.htm

**v. 6**
- Henry calls contempt for family duties a sign that a whole society is corrupt. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- Clarke points to Jesus quoting this verse in Matthew 10. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-6.html
- The ESV Study Bible, as quoted by Precept Austin, says this family betrayal looks ahead to the family splits caused by opposition to Christ (Matt 10:35–36). Precept Austin also quotes Leslie Allen: people need a stable inner circle to stay balanced, and here even that is gone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_7_commentary
- In a sermon, John Piper says Micah sees his sons turning against him and his daughters against his wife. He then shows Jesus using the verse to describe what His coming brings. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/parenting-with-hope-in-the-worst-of-times
- Coffman says sin breaks every bond, and the same happened in the persecutions of the gospel era. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-6.html

**v. 7**
- Henry says that even when we must cry "woe is me," we still have a God to look to. We should look *for* Him too, and wait for His rescue in His own way and time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- Guzik says a culture with no one trustworthy is bad. God can still use it, because it pushes us to trust the One who never fails. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- TGC's commentary says this "I" sets Micah against the corrupt officials and false prophets. The verse also links the warnings of judgment to the promise of salvation that follows. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/micah/
- Henry Morris, quoted by Precept Austin, says Micah speaks for the faithful few and trusts God alone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_7_commentary

**v. 8**
- Guzik paraphrases the verse as "you see me low now, but not for long; God will lift me up." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Calvin says it means the church is not beyond hope. God lets His people fall so that they may soon rise. He notes that "rise" is in the past tense in the Hebrew. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_jonah_micah_nahum/micah_7_8.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-8.html
- Barnes says that sitting in darkness becomes the moment the sufferer turns to God, who is their light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-8.htm
- A Biblical Illustrator sermon applies the verse to a Christian who has fallen into sin. It doesn't excuse the fall, but treats patient acceptance of God's correction as a sign of real repentance. https://biblehub.com/sermons/micah/7-8.htm
- The BibleHub study page links the verse to Proverbs 24:16 and Psalm 27:1. https://biblehub.com/study/micah/7-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan on the difference between remorse and repentance. Remorse is sorry for itself because sin brought pain. Repentance grieves the wrong done to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Henry says a truly sorry person accepts trouble patiently. When we complain to God about bad times, we should first complain about our own hearts. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- Calvin says the church relies on two things: it admits it deserves God's anger, and it trusts God to take up its case against its enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-9.html
- Poole says the faithful few declare God just, because their sins deserved even worse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-9.htm

**v. 10**
- TGC's commentary says that in vv. 8–10 "Lady Jerusalem" speaks to her enemy, "Lady Nineveh." She names the LORD in every verse, last of all in the enemy's mocking question "Where is the LORD your God?" https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/micah/
- Whedon reads these lines as the hopeful remnant expressing confidence. The enemy will be trampled like mud in the street (compare Isa 10:6) and the remnant lifted up. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/micah-7.html
- Henry says the church's cause may seem lost for a time, but God will plead it in the end and judge her enemies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik says God will send out a wide call to gather and restore His people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- TGC's commentary says Jerusalem's walls will be rebuilt and her borders pushed out from Egypt to Assyria. It adds that the Hebrew name for Egypt used here literally means "Affliction Place." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/micah/
- Clarke's outline calls this a prediction of great prosperity and growth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/micah-7.html
- The BibleHub study page applies v. 11 to God enlarging His kingdom today. https://biblehub.com/micah/7.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik says the returning people will find a land ruined by judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Henry, using the margin's reading, says rescue comes only *after* the land has lain desolate, and the people's sin is what made it desolate. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- TGC's commentary also points to the people's wickedness as the cause of the wasteland. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/micah/

**v. 14**
- Henry calls this a prophetic prayer that works like a promise. Israel is God's flock and His inheritance. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- A shorter version of Henry applies the prayer to Christ as the great Shepherd of the church, which lives "in a wood": in the world but not of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/micah/7.htm
- TGC's commentary pictures the elect sheep in a forest-like orchard, as before they rebelled. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/micah/

**v. 15**
- Guzik says the close relationship of the old days will be restored, and wonders will grow out of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- TGC's commentary says God will care for His sheep as in the Exodus, when He fed them manna. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/micah/
- Henry says God will repeat the miracles of earlier ages. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/micah/7.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- Guzik says the hostile nations will see they were wrong, and will come to respect the LORD as they never had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- The BibleHub chapter study notes that Assyrian carvings show defeated kings crawling before the emperor. Micah turns that image around: here the pagan nations crawl before Israel's God. https://biblehub.com/micah/7.htm
- The Bridgeway commentary says the nations will stop fighting Israel and humbly submit to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-6.html

**v. 18**
- Guzik quotes Boice: the verse plays on Micah's own name, which means "Who is like Yahweh?" Guzik also says God's reasons for mercy lie in Himself. His judgments are like cancer surgery: painful but needed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Barnes says no false god was ever claimed to forgive freely. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-18.html
- Calvin says God's glory shines most of all in this: He can be reconciled, and He even invites sinners to come to Him. (same URL)
- Gill says the Hebrew word for "pardon" means to lift up and carry away. He links this to sins being laid on Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-18.htm
- A sermon on BibleHub reads it as "who bears iniquity." It links "passes over" to the Passover in Egypt. https://biblehub.com/sermons/micah/7-18.htm
- Clarke says judgment is God's "strange work"; He would rather save than destroy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/micah-7.html
- Guzik and the BibleHub study page draw the same lesson: people God has forgiven must forgive others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/ and https://biblehub.com/study/micah/7-18.htm

**v. 19**
- Keil & Delitzsch say God will "tread down" sin as an enemy and drown it, as He drowned Pharaoh in the sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-19.htm
- TGC's commentary also links the verse to Exodus 14–15. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/micah/
- Henry says that when God forgives sin, He also breaks its power. He throws sins into the deep sea, not the shallows, where they might wash back up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/micah/7.htm
- Guzik says God's forgiveness has no probation period, and he adds his "No Fishing" sign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Gill says God's eye still sees the sins, but His justice no longer punishes them, because Christ has satisfied it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-19.html
- JFB explains why the verse changes from "our" to "their": Micah first counts himself among the people, then speaks about them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-19.htm

**v. 20**
- Guzik says God gives His people truth as well as mercy. The love shown to the fathers is still available to anyone who receives it by faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Henry says the book ends with praise for God's faithfulness to His covenant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- The BibleHub study page says God's sworn promises are sure. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/micah/7.htm

## Part 2: Where Protestant teachers differ

**v. 4: Who are the "watchmen"?**
- Most read them as the true prophets who warned of judgment: Barnes, Coffman, Constable, and Keil & Delitzsch. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-4.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-4.htm
- Calvin (Reformed) reads them as the *false* prophets, whose flattery misled people and rulers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-4.html

**vv. 8–10: Who is the enemy?**
- Barnes says Babylon and Edom, and in every age, devils or evil men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-8.htm
- Clarke says Assyria and Chaldea. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-8.html
- TGC says Nineveh. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/micah/

**vv. 9–20: Spiritual Israel and the church, or national Israel's future?**
- Coffman (Restoration Movement, Arminian) says the promises to Abraham always belonged to his *spiritual* children. He adds that the prophets didn't always understand their own message (1 Pet 1:10–12). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/micah-7.html
- Calvin speaks of "the Church" throughout. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-9.html
- Henry applies v. 14 to Christ and the church. He also mentions a future restoration of Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/micah/7.htm
- Smith's Bible Commentary says the "indignation" in v. 9 always means the coming Tribulation, and that God will restore Israel as a nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-8.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-19.html
- Gerrish's *Light of Israel* (non-denominational, Arminian) says most commentators skip this section because they miss God's work in modern Israel, and he blames lingering antisemitism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-10.html

**v. 18: Who receives this pardon?**
- Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) says the "remnant" are those chosen by grace, redeemed by Christ, and brought to repent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-18.htm
- Calvin says the pardon is for God's heritage and His elect. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-18.html
- Henry says God stays angry forever with those who are unpardoned. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_007.cfm
- Guzik stresses that God opens His hand of mercy to all who will receive it. The only sin that can't be forgiven is rejecting that mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-7/
- Clarke says God is ready to save whenever sinners return. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/micah-7.html

**vv. 9 and 19: Does a forgiven sinner still face punishment?**
- Calvin says v. 19 teaches full forgiveness. He attacks the Catholic idea that God forgives the sin but keeps the punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-19.html
- Barnes says God removes the eternal penalty at once, yet punishment often follows a forgiven sinner through life as an "austere form of His love." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-9.htm
- Barnes also says on v. 19 that every sin is pardoned "through Baptism and on Repentance." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/7-19.html

**v. 9: Who "pleads my case"?**
- Gill identifies the advocate as Christ the Mediator. He mentions Gussetius, who took the verb in the sense of offering a sacrifice for sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-9.htm

## Part 3: Other views (limited)

- **Modern scholarship:**
  - Whedon reports that scholars disagree over who speaks in vv. 1–6. Some say the prophet, some Zion, some the "true Israel." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/micah-7.html
  - Coffman reports that some critics cut vv. 8ff. or credit them to an editor after the exile. He rejects this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/micah-7.html
  - The NET Bible translates v. 4 differently: "the day you try to avoid by posting watchmen." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/micah/7-4.html
- **Catholic and patristic:**
  - I couldn't reach newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
  - The only early-church voices I found are quotations on a Protestant page. Jerome says examples of children turning on parents are sadly too common to need listing. Dionysius advises caution rather than suspicion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/7-6.htm
  - Calvin's remark about Catholic teaching on punishment (above) is his own polemic, not a Catholic source.
- **Popular modern teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** I found nothing on these sites about Micah 7.
